interest: This document provides a valuable administrative overview of U.S. diplomatic monitoring of Japanese financial instability during two pivotal historical moments: the immediate aftermath of the Mukden Incident in autumn 1931, and Japan's withdrawal from the League of Nations in early 1933. The cross-references highlight how international and domestic political crises directly rattled Japanese financial markets, causing emergency exchange closures and wiping out hundreds of millions of yen in securities value. For researchers of interwar Japanese economic history, this list of papers serves as an essential pointer to detailed periodic reports filed elsewhere in the Department of State decimal archives under 894.00 P.R.
overview: This file consists of a Department of State List of Papers sheet (Form DS-46) under subject classification 894.5171 (Financial Conditions. Budget. Dept. Bond Issues. Loans. Public Securities. Credits., Exchanges., Japan, Stock.). The sheet records two cross-reference entries directing researchers to periodic reports filed under decimal file 894.00 P.R. The first entry references despatch No. 351 of October 9, 1931, forwarded from Japan by Edwin L. Neville, concerning the emergency closure and suspension of trading on the Tokyo Stock Exchange between September 25 and September 28, 1931. The second entry, dated March 6, 1933, references a report under Ambassador Joseph C. Grew documenting the dramatic collapse of the Tokyo stock market that began on February 14, 1933, which erased approximately half a billion yen in security valuations by the end of that month.

subfiles.about: A Department of State list of papers cross-referencing diplomatic despatches and periodic reports regarding Japanese stock market suspensions and crashes in 1931 and 1933.
subfiles.summary: This document is a Department of State List of Papers (Form DS-46) indexing correspondence on stock exchanges in Japan under decimal file 894.5171. It cross-references an October 9, 1931 report from Edwin L. Neville regarding the temporary closure and suspension of trading on the Tokyo Stock Exchange from September 25 to 28, 1931. It also cites a March 6, 1933 report under Ambassador Joseph C. Grew detailing the February 1933 Tokyo stock market collapse, during which security values dropped by approximately 500 million yen.
